newsitem.title: USA: U.S. April leading index posts first fall in a year.
newsitem.headline: U.S. April leading index posts first fall in a year.

text.p: A key gauge of national economic activity posted its first drop in more than a year during April, the Conference Board said on Tuesday, a sign of potentially slower growth in coming months.

The Index of Leading Indicators, which is supposed to forecast economic trends six to nine months ahead, fell by 0.1 percent in April -- its first decline since a 0.7 percent fall in January 1996 -- after a revised 0.2 percent rise in March.
The private Conference Board said six out of 10 separate measures of economic activity that make up the leading index weakened in April.

The biggest negative contribution came from increased weekly applications to state unemployment insurance programmes, but lower stock prices and fewer new orders for capital goods also put a drag on the index.

In addition, vendor delivery times were faster, an indication that factories were not as busy, and consumer expectations were not as bright in April as they were in March. There also were fewer new applications for building permits.
Only four indicators were higher in April.
The average workweek lengthened, consumer goods orders picked up from March, the money supply increased and the Treasury yield curve was more favourable.
Previously, the Conference Board said the leading index had risen 0.1 percent in March but it revised that up marginally.

The latest report adds to recent mixed signs about the economy's direction. It fits with government reports that showed weaker retail-store sales in April and flat levels of industrial output, as well as a softening in used-car prices and lackluster new-car sales by U.S. automakers.
But on Monday, the National Association of Purchasing Managers said its index of indurstrial activity unexpectedly surged in May even as consumer spending was showing signs of easing.

The conflicting signs about the economy's vigour left analysts uncertain about the extent of a predicted slowdown in the expansion from the first quarter's sizzling 5.8 percent annual pace, though the pace of growth is widely expected to ease significantly as the year wears on.
